description:
We are building a CubeSat mission design simulator for the Space Mission Design Game challenge. The goal is to let players design and launch a satellite while balancing real constraints like power, mass, budget, and orbital mechanics, paired with a simple hardware prototype.

We already have the engineering, CAD, and simulation logic covered, so we are mainly looking for a frontend/web developer or UI/UX designer to help us build a clean interface. Reach out if you want to team up!
summary:
CUBETRONIX built CubeSat Flight School, an interactive web game that teaches the basics of CubeSat design and operation by letting players build a real satellite under real engineering constraints. Players select components — structure, solar arrays, battery, on-board computer, payload, propulsion, and attitude sensors — and the game validates their design in real time against mass, power, eclipse-survival, RF link margin, and downlink throughput budgets, mirroring the trade-offs actual mission engineers face. Once a design passes pre-flight checks, players fly their CubeSat through a live orbital mission with telemetry, thruster burns, and image capture.

To make the experience tangible beyond the screen, we built a physical ground-station controller using a Raspberry Pi Pico: a joystick to pan camera views, an ultrasonic sensor and IMU to pilot the spacecraft with hand motion, a launch button to fire thrusters or capture images, and LEDs/buzzer for live mission feedback — connected to the browser via Web Serial.

This matters because space engineering can feel abstract and inaccessible to students. By turning CubeSat design into a hands-on, physically interactive game, we hope to lower the barrier to engaging with real aerospace engineering concepts for younger students and newcomers to the field.
details:
CubeSat Flight School is a two-part system: a web-based mission simulator and a physical ground-station controller, built together so players can both design a satellite and physically control it.

What it does. In the browser, players build a CubeSat by choosing real components (structure, solar arrays, battery, on-board computer, payload, propulsion, attitude sensors) from a catalog. A live engineering model checks the design against mass, power generation, eclipse battery reserve, RF link margin, and downlink throughput — the same budgets real CubeSat teams juggle. Once the design clears pre-flight checks, the player launches into an orbital mission with live telemetry, camera views, thruster burns, and image-capture objectives.

The hardware layer. We built a handheld ground-station controller around a Raspberry Pi Pico (RP2350), running MicroPython: a joystick cycles camera views, an HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor and MPU6050 IMU let you physically tilt and move to steer the spacecraft’s point-of-view, a LAUNCH button fires thrusters or captures images, and two LEDs plus a buzzer give live mission feedback — red/green LEDs mirror the spacecraft’s actual solar-eclipse and battery state in the simulation, and the buzzer confirms captures, burns, and mission outcomes. The Pico talks to the browser over the Web Serial API, with no backend server in between.

Benefits and impact. Most CubeSat education is either purely theoretical or locked behind expensive lab hardware. By pairing an accurate engineering simulation with an affordable, physically interactive controller, we lower the barrier for students to build intuition for real spacecraft design trade-offs and orbital operations — hands-on, not just on a slide.

Tools and stack. React + Vite + Tailwind CSS for the web app, Three.js-based 3D rendering for the CubeSat and orbital views, the Web Serial API for the browser-hardware bridge, and MicroPython on a Raspberry Pi Pico 2 (RP2350) for the ground-station firmware (direct I2C register reads for the IMU, a complementary filter for orientation).

Creativity and design considerations. The creative core is closing the loop between a digital engineering simulation and a tactile, game-like controller — you don’t just click “launch,” you physically aim a satellite with your hand. We also had to account for things like serial-port contention between the dev tooling and the browser, and designing LED/buzzer feedback that’s meaningful rather than decorative (eclipse and battery state drive LED color, not just an on/off blink).
